day_phrase: the day this person's state has set for choosing presidential electors (states choose on different days, from 1 November until the electors meet on 4 December 1816)

descriptors.R: a senator from New York and former minister to Britain, backed by the opposition party's electors without a formal nomination
descriptors.D: the Secretary of State, who also ran the War Department in the late war with Britain, nominated by the administration party's congressional caucus

compile_desc.R: the opposition party, which held the presidency from 1789 to 1801
compile_desc.D: the party of the administration in office since 1801

others_line: A few unpledged elector tickets on some ballots (answer "other").
never_name: King, Monroe, Tompkins, Madison, Crawford or John Eager Howard

slice_sources.men: 1810 and 1820 census interpolated to 1816, free adult men outside the Southern states; the census gives free white males in bands (16–26, 26–45, 45+), so men 21+ are split from the 16–26 band. Voters were men meeting each state's rules: many states still required property or taxpaying qualifications (Virginia and Rhode Island a freehold). Electors were chosen by popular vote in 10 states; elsewhere (Connecticut, Delaware, Georgia, Indiana, Louisiana, Massachusetts, New York, South Carolina and Vermont) men cast no presidential vote. Free Black men could vote in some Northern states on the same or stricter terms.
slice_sources.women: 1810 and 1820 census interpolated to 1816, women 21+ (estimated from age bands). No woman could vote for president this year: New Jersey had ended women's voting in 1807. Turnout is zero by law, not by estimate.
slice_sources.south-white: 1810 and 1820 census interpolated to 1816, white adults in Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, Tennessee and Louisiana; only men meeting their state's property or taxpaying rules could vote (Virginia required a freehold). The South Carolina, Georgia and Louisiana legislatures chose their electors, so people there cast no presidential vote.
slice_sources.black-south: 1810 and 1820 census interpolated to 1816, Black adults in Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, Tennessee and Louisiana; the census gives free people of colour without age or sex before 1820, so adults are estimated. The great majority were enslaved and could not vote. Free Black men meeting the property tests could legally vote only in North Carolina (until its 1835 constitution) and Tennessee (until its 1834 constitution); the other Southern states limited the vote to white men. In South Carolina, Georgia and Louisiana the legislature chose the electors, so no one there voted for president directly.
slice_sources.immigrants: No source: before 1850 the census recorded no nativity, and the 1810 and 1820 censuses did not count aliens. Immigration was small (a few thousand a year), naturalization needed five years' residence under the 1802 act, and aliens could not vote in most states; any slice here is an assumption, not a measurement.
